title: Sydney Sweeney advert sparks backlash from female athletes: ‘This is what women in sport look like’
content:
A controversial sports gambling advert featuring Sydney Sweeney has sparked a backlash among female athletes for sexualising women in sports.

The American actress, 29, is an equity holder and strategic partner in Novig, a federally regulated U.S. prediction market that lets users trade contracts on sporting outcomes. Its “Just Sports” campaign shows an otherwise naked Sweeney covering herself with American footballs, basketballs and hockey pads while pitching Novig as a sports-only alternative to markets that also offer contracts on politics, wars and death.

The advert predictably went viral but has provoked criticism from female athletes for objectifying women.

“Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like,” British sprinter Amy Hunt said during a live BBC interview after finishing fourth in the 200 metres at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Sunday. “21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening,” Hunt added, referring to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden’s winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth-fastest women’s 200m in history.

In a post on her Instagram, four-time Olympic swimming champion Ariarne Titmus described the Novig advert as a “kick in the face” to women who had dedicated their lives to their sport and questioned why women’s bodies and women’s sport were still being sexualised.

The criticism has developed into a wider social-media response with former UCLA gymnast Gracie Kramer posting competition footage in a now expired Instagram story under the message “this is what a woman in sport looks like”, while Olympic swimmer Lani Pallister and sprinter Bree Rizzo shared footage on the social media platform from their own careers.

Olympic track cycling champion Sophie Capewell, Wales rugby international Lisa Neumann, Team GB rugby player Ellie Boatman and Australian water polo Olympic silver medallist Tilly Kearns have also responded. Kearns wrote that she “absolutely hated” the advert, while world champion boxer Skye Nicolson criticised the use of sexuality to market sport.

The Australian Institute of Sport joined the response with footage of women in archery, gymnastics, boxing, softball and sports science under the message “THIS is sport”.

The row comes as prediction-market companies spend heavily on celebrity-led advertising around the start of the NFL season. A Polymarket campaign has featured LeBron James, Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Rajon Rondo, Reggie Bush, Spike Lee and model Emily Ratajkowski, while rival Betr reunited Entourage actors Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier for its own promotion.

Sweeney has not directly addressed the athletes’ criticism. Amid the backlash, however, she shared images from previous nude sports photoshoots featuring Serena Williams, Ronda Rousey, Rob Gronkowski and Karl-Anthony Towns on Instagram.

Novig launched its nationwide sports prediction market in August after receiving designation from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

Founder and chief executive Jacob Fortinsky told Front Office Sports after the campaign launched that Sweeney had approached the company about an equity partnership and helped craft its message.

“Sydney is great at captivating audiences and being the centre of attention,” Fortinsky said. “In some sense, it forces us into the national discourse.”

Fortinsky defended the adult nature of the campaign by noting that Novig is restricted to users aged 21 and over.

Sweeney told Complex she was involved in creative conversations around the Novig campaign “from the very beginning” and that the advert’s concept was “a very simple and playful idea.”

Further Novig campaigns featuring Sweeney are planned, including one focused on responsible trading.

This is not the first time an advert featuring Sweeney has attracted controversy.

In 2025, American Eagle’s “Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans” campaign used a play on “jeans” and “genes”, including references to the blond, blue-eyed actor’s inherited traits. Some critics accused the campaign of invoking white supremacy, while U.S. President Donald Trump publicly praised it. Sweeney returned to American Eagle for another denim campaign in April.

Speaking to GQ, Sweeney said she had been unaware of the controversy at the time as she had been filming Euphoria. “I knew at the end of the day what that ad was for, and it was great jeans,” she said. “It didn’t affect me one way or the other.”

In an interview with the Wall Street Journal, American Eagle CEO Jay Schottenstein defended the campaign saying: “We stand behind what we did.”
